units.en: A ⟦0⟧ is an important tool that helps players visualize how their divisions will advance, allows the AI to control the player's divisions automatically, and can confer a ⟦1⟧. Plans do not have to be drawn in order to give divisions orders, but are generally recommended as they reduce micromanagement, improve the flow of gameplay and provide bonuses to unit performance that can offset those enjoyed by heavily ⟦2⟧ enemies.

If desired, different divisions within a single army may be allocated to different battle plans. In this case, players will usually have to manually assign divisions to each front, or they will default to the first front drawn.

An example of a battle plan would be a major invasion of Italy, north of enemy lines, designed to crush an enemy preoccupied with an engagement from the south. The player can set up and separately activate one or more amphibious landings, paradrops, and attacks by ground forces already facing the enemy, each at the time they think best. Some of these plan orders might be set up to be implemented by the player at the same time, while others may be set up to occur in sequence, in each case activated by the player as needed by shift-clicking only on that specific order to activate it, and with the ability to change that element of the plan or the troops assigned to it before or after activation. This allows different parts of an army to perform separate tasks for the player within an overall strategy, much as army corps performed different missions for WW2 armies. Use of such complex plans is optional, but occasionally very useful when a player has to launch multiple different operations at the same time or by stages.

To make a battle plan for offensive land operations, the player must first define a ⟦0⟧ – this is the point from which the army group will begin operations. Select the Front Line button or press ⟦1⟧, then click on or draw a line on the map along a national border or the current line between opposing forces to indicate where the army's currently selected divisions will assemble. Then click the ⟦2⟧ button (a line with an arrow) or press ⟦3⟧ and draw the front to which the armies should advance from the current Front Line.
The battle plan tools can be accessed via the ⟦0⟧ that opens when an army (a general) or an army group (a field marshal) is selected.

A naval invasion is an amphibious attack on enemy territory. It is a very powerful tool to open up new fronts against an enemy where they least expect them.

When selecting a naval invasion order, the player will be asked to left-click on a province with a ⟦0⟧ as a point of departure and right-click on the enemy province(s) to invade. The army will automatically gather at the naval base they will depart from for the assault.

Naval invasions may be launched from any friendly port that the player has access to. This means that an invasion of enemy territory can be launched from the port of an ally that is not at war with the enemy.
A naval invasion is constrained by two separate caps:
the ⟦0⟧ — maximum number of divisions per single naval invasion order, and
the ⟦0⟧ — maximum number of naval invasion orders that may be prepared at the same time.

The base values are ⟦0⟧ per order and ⟦1⟧ at a time. Both caps are raised by researching naval transport technology. Without ⟦2⟧, these come from the base ⟦3⟧ tech tree; with Man the Guns, they come from the equivalent ⟦4⟧ tree.
⟦0⟧ Amphibious Invasion; ⟦1⟧ Invasion Defense; ⟦2⟧ prep days

Selecting either ⟦0⟧ or ⟦1⟧ in the ⟦2⟧ special-forces tree grants ⟦3⟧ additional division cap and ⟦4⟧ additional plan cap respectively. Several national focuses, ideas and Military Industrial Organisations also grant invasion-cap modifiers.

A naval invasion order with more divisions assigned than the division cap will not take place. The arrow on the map appears but with the text ⟦0⟧. The assigned divisions keep their ⟦1⟧ exclamation mark which indicates that they have no orders.

A country's invasion capacity is measured in division count, not total weight or combat width. Wider and more powerful division templates allow players to execute stronger invasions, at the cost of more convoys (see ⟦0⟧).

Naval invasions require time to prepare before they may be executed. The exact time it will take is dependent on technology and the amount of divisions to be shipped over. With only the first level of naval invasion technology, a 1-division invasion will take 7 days and a 10-division invasion will take 70 days of planning. ⟦0⟧ technology (1940) and ⟦1⟧ (1944) further reduce the required time, as do ⟦2⟧ and ⟦3⟧ land doctrines and the ⟦4⟧ fleet-in-being subdoctrine.
The planning will proceed immediately, even while the divisions are still on their way to the departure port.

It is possible to prepare several invasions from different ports in parallel, even to the same target province(s), saving on total preparation time, as long as the plan cap is not exceeded. It is also possible to prepare several invasions to different target provinces from the same port.

In order to ship units over to foreign lands, sufficient convoys are required to do so. The amount of convoys an individual division requires is dependent on its ⟦0⟧; the weight is equivalent with the amount of convoys required to ship over one division. The amount of convoys required is rounded up. Technology may decrease the amount of convoys required for an invasion.

The actual value of ⟦0⟧ of a seazone can be seen in the seazone property window, that you get when you click a seazone. You have to hover with the mouse over the naval supremacy bar. Alternatively you can see it, when you hover with your mouse over a seazone in the ⟦1⟧ (accessible with the ⟦2⟧ button).

The ⟦0⟧ of a seazone is calculated from the intel you have from nations you are ⟦1⟧ and that ⟦2⟧ in that seazone. If you are not at war, you have 100% ⟦3⟧ everywhere. If you are at war with one country, you have 100% ⟦4⟧ in all seazones in which this country has no ships assigned (the value ⟦5⟧ is 0). In the seazones in which the country has ships assigned (⟦6⟧ > 0), the ⟦7⟧ is the intel you have of that country. If you are at war with more countries, and more than one of these countries have ships in one seazone, the ⟦8⟧ is weighted towards the country that has more naval supremacy in that seazone.

To ⟦0⟧ a naval invasion, a country requires ⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧ (also called 'naval superiority' in some tooltips) ⟦3⟧ (sea zones) in which the divisions will need to traverse the sea en-route to their destination. These are the regions the arrow of the naval invasion battle plan passes through.

Per-ship supremacy scales with the ship's production cost and manpower; the exact constants are not currently exposed in ⟦6⟧ and are determined by the engine.
Task forces with ⟦0⟧ order do not contribute to ⟦1⟧.

⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧ provide a bonus to ⟦2⟧. The maximum possible bonus from air superiority is +100% to the ship amount, making each ship count for two. It is achieved when air superiority is 100% and there are enough planes to cover 100% of the sea region.

⟦0⟧ is only required for a ⟦1⟧ to launch the prepared invasion. After that the invasion will ⟦2⟧. Once the naval invasion has been properly planned, ⟦3⟧ and ⟦4⟧ have been attained, and sufficient convoys are gathered, the plan may be activated.

Invading divisions travel through the sea province by province on convoys, and can be intercepted by enemy fleets and bombers just like supply and trade convoys. It is recommended to use escorts for the convoys, lest the enemy rally their entire fleet to intercept the invading fleet.
When invaders reach the shores and begin to disembark, the side being invaded gets a notification with an icon and a sound and has a brief moment to rally any defenders.
Invasion speed is improved by technology, and is greatly delayed by attacks on the convoys.

If the invasion meets resistance, similar to attacking over a naval strait, the landing troops receive a default ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧ penalty to attack and breakthrough in the ensuing combat (see ⟦2⟧). The Amphibious adjuster of the division can modify this penalty. Heavy equipment generally makes it worse, while marines, engineers, amphibious vehicles, and flame tanks perform better (see ⟦3⟧).
Consider using ⟦0⟧ to support the invasion, as well as any ⟦1⟧ in range.
